2.text: instance, on a village shore, — they simply seize the boat by the lashings and

3.text: carry it along, cargo and all. These methods of landing, quite impracticable

4.text: with the ordinary wooden whale-boat, look strange to a civilized eye; but when,

5.text: in the first heavy surf encountered on our journey, we tried to land with the

6.text: bow forward, in the ordinary way, the boat filled with water and nearly

7.text: capsized; and it would have been completely wrecked had it not been for the

8.text: extreme toughness and elasticity of its frame.

9.text: Of the wooden boats I had occasion to see, the “sampan” of northern

10.text: Japanese fishermen with flat bottom and smooth sides, more nearly resembles

11.text: the skin boat. Like that, it is able to land through surf, when ordinary

12.text: European boats are threatened at every attempt with capsizing.

13.text: For setting out from shore, the skin boat is put close to the water, with

14.text: bow foremost but out of reach of the larger waves. Two or three inflated

15.text: floats are laid under it, with long lines tied to their flippers. Then the boat

16.text: is loaded, and with one effort pushed into the water; while the crew, with

17.text: oars and poles, prevent it from being hurled against the shore.

18.text: On narrow strips of land between two shores the boats are unloaded and

19.text: taken across. Six men can easily carry on their shoulders an empty boat,

20.text: even when soaked with water. Sometimes only part of the freight is taken

21.text: out, and the boat is pushed across on the floats, which act like rollers and

22.text: prevent its contact with the ground.

23.text: One of the drawbacks of the skin boat is the fragility of its cover. Every

24.text: sharp stone is liable to cut a hole through it, especially when it has been

25.text: soaked and softened with water. At every landing it is necessary to look

26.text: carefully over the whole skin surface, to clean away from under the central

27.text: timber every small pebble, and to patch even the minutest hole; otherwise

28.text: the boat may suddenly spring a leak while on the water, and necessitate an

29.text: extra landing. When in good repair, the boat is water-tight, and requires no

30.text: bailer; on the other hand, I know of cases where, on account of an over-

31.text: looked gap, boats were almost sunk before a landing could be effected. While

32.text: on shore, the boat is turned upside down, pebbles and sand are shaken off by

33.text: repeated blows with the oar, and the cover is allowed to dry. If not dried

34.text: for a long time, the boat will warp and get out of shape. To prevent warping,

35.text: the boat has several sets of special lashings (see Fig. 44, c¹), which connect

36.text: the gunwales with the central timber, and can be lengthened or shortened.

37.text: The Reindeer Chukchee living near the seashore also use skin boats;

38.text: and the boats of the Telqäˊp people, for instance, are just as large as those

39.text: of the Maritime villagers. The inland Reindeer people have no boats, and

40.text: hardly need any. A few of them buy from the Russianized Yukaghir or from

41.text: the Yakut small wooden canoes, and drag them along to use in summer on the
